findings.title: Session-cookie prefix pollution can skip revocation while the logout handler reports success
findings.codeObservation: The application's readAuthCookie accepts only the exact session cookie or numbered chunks. Auth.js SessionStore collects every cookie name beginning with the session-cookie prefix. The logout branch checked logoutFailed/unavailable but did not check frameworkFailed. Thus a valid base cookie plus a non-chunk prefix cookie reaches Auth.js as a concatenated invalid JWE; Auth.js logs the decode error and skips its signOut event, but its raw result still contains the logout redirect and cookie clearing.

method: The inline script imported the installed real @auth/core encode/decode, SessionStore and signOut implementations.
It generated a synthetic random signing secret and random opaque session token in memory, then used real Auth.js encode to create a valid encrypted session cookie.
It initialized SessionStore with that base cookie plus the non-chunk cookie name authjs.session-token-foreign carrying a fixed non-secret test value.
It invoked real signOut with a counter in events.signOut and a separate counter in logger.error, then decrypted the original base cookie again.
Only safe booleans, event counts, the fixed local redirect path and cleared cookie names were printed. No database was connected.
reproduction.evidenceBoundary: The event omission and raw Auth.js result were directly observed. The application's success response and persistence of an ACTIVE database row were inferred from the reviewed handler/event code, not observed in a PostgreSQL run.

findings.recommendedVerification: Exercise the real HTTP handler with a valid session and an extra prefix cookie. A successful logout must revoke the original database session before clearing cookies; a framework failure must return a safe failure. Reuse the original cookie against the real database guard to verify the resulting state.

findings.title: A valid transport proof could be replayed for the same method and target during its validity window
findings.codeObservation: The reviewed verifier validated HMAC, method, target and a 30-second timestamp window, but did not bind the proof to a currently active request context or consume its nonce.

method: The inline script loaded the actual src/server/ingress.ts through createRequire and tsx.
It created an ephemeral loopback HTTP server on an automatically assigned port and generated a random synthetic HMAC secret in memory.
The test-only server stamped the real IncomingMessage with stampTrustedRequest and returned that synthetic proof to the test driver.
The driver constructed two separate Request objects using the same POST method, auth callback target and captured proof, then called verifyTrustedRequest on both.
The production application was not modified to reflect proofs. The ephemeral server was closed after the observation.
reproduction.evidenceBoundary: Same-proof replay at the internal verification boundary was directly observed. The production Node ingress overwrites caller-supplied proofs, so this review did not demonstrate a public-network address-forgery or throttle-bypass exploit.

findings.recommendedVerification: Require a live request-bound context and single consumption. Verify first-use acceptance, second-use rejection, replay in a different request context, cross-request concurrency isolation, and rejection after the original request context is absent.

findings.title: The logout UI claimed local cookie clearing for every 503 response
findings.codeObservation: LogoutButton treated any HTTP 503 as proof that local login cookies had been cleared and disabled retry. The custom Node ingress and generic request-handler failure paths can return 503 without any Set-Cookie clearing header. Therefore status alone does not prove local clearing.

method: Read the LogoutButton 503 branch and the custom server's generic 503 response paths.

findings.recommendedVerification: Only show the local-clearing message after a dedicated response receipt from the Auth.js wrapper's cookie-clearing path. For a generic ingress/proxy 503 without that receipt, retain a safe retryable failure. Cover both responses in UI tests.

additionalObservation.description: The browser test queried LOGIN_SUCCESS by actorId, while the credentials service deliberately records a SYSTEM actor with the successful User in targetId. This mismatch was reported to the UI agent. The UI agent stated that it would align the assertion; this report does not claim the revised browser test passed.

repairStatusAtRecording.ingress: The main agent reported a request-bound AsyncLocalStorage and one-time consumption fix; the updated code was read while preparing this report. The preliminary reproduction was not rerun against that fix in this review.
repairStatusAtRecording.logoutAndUi: The UI agent was assigned strict logout-cookie handling and an explicit local-clearing receipt. Their final code and execution evidence have not been independently verified here.
repairStatusAtRecording.overall: Fixes in progress do not change this historical FAIL decision.

limitations: No PostgreSQL integration scenario, mutation suite, browser run or complete Phase011 Gate was executed by this reviewer in this preliminary review.
No original reviewed-source hashes were captured; exact pre-fix source bytes cannot be reconstructed from this report alone.
No full application HTTP logout reproduction was executed. AUTH011-SEC-01 clearly distinguishes the real Auth.js observation from application/database consequences inferred from source.

The code review found no other direct bypass in dual-bucket admission, the dummy bcrypt path, or per-request database role/status/sessionVersion checks; this is not a proof that those areas pass their required dynamic cases.
Final closure requires a new attempt with the fixes, the original targeted regressions and independent review of actual database/browser/Gate evidence.
